question: Do the relative populations of geometrically distinct velocity-segment shapes change through the inertial-range cascade, or is small-scale isotropic turbulence as diverse in normalized eddy shape as large-scale turbulence?

key_findings.claim: The paper defines an eddy as a velocity segment in a one-dimensional window and quotients segments by spatial dilation, velocity multiplication, and velocity offset to obtain geometric equivalence classes.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 2 declares two segments equivalent when one becomes the other after rescaling the observation length and applying an affine transform in velocity. The construction intentionally covers every sampled segment and ignores eddy dynamics and interactions.

key_findings.claim: Finite-sample proxy classes are represented by ratios of successive velocity increments, which remove amplitude and offset information and encode local segment shape.
key_findings.evidence: For n evenly spaced points, equation 4 forms an n-2 dimensional vector of arctangents of adjacent-increment ratios. Segments with the same vector belong to the same n-point equivalence class; increasing n is asserted to refine the class toward the full velocity-segment equivalence class.

key_findings.claim: Selected normalized-shape moments are empirically flat across the inertial range in one isotropic-turbulence DNS.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4 plots even moments p=2,4,6,8 of the three-point angle feature for a 1024-cubed periodic-box simulation at Taylor Reynolds number 433 and shows an approximately l^0 region between the marked cut-off and inertial-range limits. Figure 5 adds several mixed seven-point statistics at Reynolds number 344.

key_findings.claim: Under a finite-class power-law mixture model, scale-invariant enough feature moments imply scale-invariant weights for the proxy equivalence classes.
key_findings.evidence: The main-text argument lets the largest nonnegative exponent dominate a moment sum. The appendix treats two classes without the sign assumption by inverting a two-by-two moment matrix at two lengths and says n distinct classes require moments through order 2n.

key_findings.claim: The headline conclusion for every full eddy class is not identified by the finite-resolution evidence as written.
key_findings.evidence: Only a finite collection of moments and feature coordinates is plotted, while the number of geometric classes may be arbitrarily large or continuous. The finite-class Vandermonde-style inversion needs enough distinct moments and nondegenerate feature values; proxy features can collapse different classes. Finally, scale invariance for each finite n is passed to an n-to-infinity class limit without a uniform-convergence or measure-identification argument.

anchors.section: Step from finite n to equation 14

key_findings.claim: Scale-invariant normalized shape diversity can coexist with strong small-scale intermittency in amplitudes and dissipation.
key_findings.evidence: The equivalence relation explicitly removes velocity scale and offset, so it does not measure the volume fraction or intensity of high-vorticity and high-dissipation events directly. Contemporary DNS work finds Reynolds-dependent extreme dissipation and enstrophy even while this paper's angle features may remain invariant.

method.core_idea: Replace the intractable task of enumerating all eddy types with statistics of scale- and amplitude-normalized velocity-segment shape features, then infer how latent class weights scale with window length.
method.mechanism: Sample one-dimensional velocity windows in homogeneous isotropic DNS; define affine geometric equivalence; approximate full classes using n-point angle-ratio vectors; express feature moments as mixtures over class populations; look for l^0 moment scaling through the inertial range; and pass from proxy classes to full classes as sampling density grows.
assumptions: Small-scale isotropy makes a one-dimensional window in an arbitrary direction representative.
Every class population follows a power law in normalized length through the inertial range.
The relevant class mixture is finite or identifiable from the available moments.
Distinct classes yield sufficiently distinct feature values for moment inversion.
The finite-n class refinement converges in a way that preserves scale invariance.

techniques.role: Defines eddy type after quotienting location, length, amplitude, and offset.
Creates a finite-dimensional proxy for continuous segment shape.
Connects observed feature moments to power-law class weights.
Supplies inertial-range velocity segments and moment curves.
Removes the sign assumption for a two-class example in the appendix.

evaluations.setting: 1024^3 periodic-box DNS of isotropic turbulence at Re_lambda=433
evaluations.metric: Length-scale dependence of second, fourth, sixth, and eighth moments of the three-point angle feature
evaluations.result: All four plotted moments are approximately flat in the marked inertial range.
evaluations.baseline: Alternative l^zeta behavior with nonzero class-population exponents

evaluations.metric: Five mixed absolute moments of seven-point angle features
evaluations.result: The appendix reports approximate l^0 scaling between energy-spectrum-based inertial-range markers.

evaluations.setting: Two-class analytic mixture at two arbitrary lengths
evaluations.metric: Identifiability of the two class probabilities from second and fourth moments
evaluations.result: When the feature magnitudes are nondegenerate and both moments are invariant, the two inferred weights are equal across the two lengths.
evaluations.baseline: Main-text dominant-exponent argument requiring nonnegative exponents

limitations: The empirical case rests on one archived 1024^3 isotropic DNS, with a second Reynolds number only in a supplemental feature plot.
No independent simulation, experiment, forcing protocol, or anisotropic flow is used to test universality.
The number of full eddy classes is not shown to be finite, and finitely many moments do not identify an arbitrary continuous class distribution.
The n-point feature can map geometrically different segments to the same proxy vector between sample points.
The n-to-infinity passage is asserted without a quantitative convergence or finite-resolution error bound.
Amplitude is quotiented out, so the result does not directly adjudicate intermittency of dissipation, enstrophy, or occupied volume.
failure_modes: Different class populations can share the same finite set of angle-feature moments.
Zero or nearly zero adjacent increments make ratio features singular or numerically unstable.
A short apparent plateau can reflect finite Reynolds number or chosen inertial-range boundaries rather than exact l^0 scaling.
Rare high-order shape classes may be absent from a finite DNS even if their population exponent differs.
The equivalence quotient can declare intense and weak segments the same type, hiding the very concentration phenomenon called intermittency elsewhere in turbulence.
reusable_insights: Define precisely which nuisance transformations are removed before making claims about diversity.
Use several mixed moments, not just a second-order statistic, when probing scale-dependent mixtures.
Separate normalized morphology from event amplitude and occupied volume in turbulence taxonomies.
Require an explicit identifiability theorem before inferring every latent class weight from aggregate moment scaling.
open_questions: Can characteristic functions or distributional two-sample tests replace finite moments and identify the full angle-feature law across scales?
How stable is the result across Reynolds number, forcing, flow geometry, sampling direction, and experimental noise?
Can one bound the error between n-point proxy populations and full geometric-class populations at finite eta resolution?
What joint taxonomy captures both scale-invariant normalized shapes and scale-dependent amplitude intermittency?
Do rare coherent structures have population exponents that are invisible to the reported low-order and mixed moments?

competitive_landscape.title: Extreme dissipation and intermittency in turbulence at very high Reynolds numbers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct alternative account of small-scale population concentration
competitive_landscape.difference: Elsinga et al. model volume-weighted dissipation PDFs with significant shear layers and Reynolds-dependent extreme-event scaling; this paper instead quotients velocity amplitude and asks whether normalized segment-shape class weights vary with length.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv abstract and revision record checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: Evidence for multiplicative cascades as the origin of small-scale intermittency in turbulence
competitive_landscape.difference: Vela-Martin tracks intense enstrophy and dissipation events in isotropic DNS and finds dynamics consistent with a local multiplicative cascade; this paper analyzes static normalized velocity-shape features and concludes shape-class invariance.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv abstract and revision record checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: Intermittency of turbulent velocity and scalar fields using 3D local averaging
competitive_landscape.difference: Buaria and Sreenivasan use spherical local averages up to Re_lambda=1300 and report nonzero dissipation and enstrophy intermittency exponents; this paper uses one-dimensional amplitude-normalized morphology at Re_lambda=433 and therefore addresses a different marginal of small-scale structure.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv abstract and revision record checked 2026-08-23

competitive_landscape.title: Asymptotic Exponents from Low-Reynolds-Number Flows
competitive_landscape.relationship: DNS and multifractal analysis of small-scale exponents
competitive_landscape.difference: Schumacher, Sreenivasan, and Yakhot infer anomalous high-Reynolds scaling from velocity-gradient moments and study Gaussian-to-non-Gaussian crossover; this paper proposes a new affine-invariant segment-shape observable whose selected moments appear flat in the inertial range.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv abstract and revision record checked 2026-08-23

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The work directly determines that eddy population densities are scale-invariant, establishing that small-scale turbulence retains the diversity of large-scale turbulence.
novelty_assessment.evidence: It introduces an affine geometric equivalence relation and n-point angle features, derives a moment-mixture connection, and observes flat feature moments over an inertial range in DNS.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The normalized-shape observable is original and potentially useful. The universal class-population conclusion is materially stronger than the finite-moment, finite-resolution identification argument, and should be interpreted as a hypothesis supported for selected proxy statistics rather than a completed census of all eddy types.

reviewer_notes: Read all eight extracted pages, including the full five-step derivation, DNS setup, both feature-moment figures, the sign-free two-class appendix, and references. Four primary arXiv competitors spanning cascade intermittency, extreme dissipation, 3D local averages, and gradient-moment scaling were checked on 2026-08-23.
